essex-rumi-songwriting-(2020-).html.description: Essex Rumi is an English/Hindi hip-hop and electronic music project I started in 2020, drawing on my poetry, and songwriting ideas that emerged in the previous year. It deals with personal, often introspective themes mixed with political commentary. So far, I have written, composed, produced, and engineered each track on my own (out of necessity, for better or worse). Given here are the lyrics to each track released under the artist name, in descending order of year of release. The lyrics are also available to read on Essex Rumi’s Genius page and the tracks can be found on my Spotify artist page and my YouTube channel.[Intro] Ima go get higher than an astronaut Them phonies flash-fiction-(2022-).html.title: Flash fiction (2022-)
flash-fiction-(2022-).html.description: I started writing flash fiction in earnest around 2022, having experimented with it in high school, after being exhausted writing poetry and song lyrics and wanting a more suitable medium for one-off ideas and serialised stories without aesthetic limitations. I also found the medium suitable for typeset social media posts that could be produced and digested quickly, some of which can be found on my Instagram page. Here’s all the one-shots and parts of serialisations I’ve written in the genre so far (also available to read on my Medium page) in descending order of year of writing.I grabbed and put on my worst jacket and left through the front door. It was an uninteresting five-minute walk to Gopal’s and I really needed my daily fix. “What’s up?” I asked as I approached the counter, catching his eye. “Fine Roll, cardamom, Jolt,” I recited like every other day — Gopal’s head bobbing in sync told me he knew it too, as did his nimble hands moving intuitively to serve loyally his hundredth customer of the day. “Anything else, boss?” he asked as he handed over my pre-roll and a tiny packet of flavoured cardamom, his gaze briefly meeting mine with a little smile out of camaraderie. Despite living in the same neighbourhood, Gopal and I are from very different backgrounds. He’d been growing up here for years when they started building the high-rises up north — my family shifted into ours only about three years ago, around the time it became too expensive to even breathe this air. I can tell we’re both in our twenties, but my life’s much easier than his — he has a wife and schoolchild, and I couldn’t take care of a succulent from an ex — and I’m grateful for it. I tucked the pre-roll between my darkened lips and he struck a matchstick that he carefully carried to ignite its tip. There was an empty stool inside the shop that I promptly occupied lest someone on the road recognised me — a rich haircut like mine didn’t belong in the little shops lined along the neighbourhood sewage. I extended and crossed my legs — it was one of those rare times I was the only customer at the shop — and took in a drag from the pre-roll, holding it in for a while then turning my head to the side to exhale dodging Gopal’s face; I realised a moment later he was quite into his phone screen and couldn’t care less. The speaker on that phone was unusually loud — I could tell he was scrolling through those minute-long videos from the jarring cuts in between. I focussed on minding my own business but couldn’t — the volume was hard to ignore — and overheard ’90s Filmi dialogue and music, until the unexpected yelling of what seemed like an aggressive man began to play. “Do I look like I’m afraid of jail?” the man shouted, his incredibly intimidating tone shattering my calm perception of the environment. “I’ll beat them up, go to jail, get out of jail and beat them up again,” the looped video repeated a couple times before Gopal scrolled away to more song and dance. “Where’s the — is the Jolt back in stock yet?” I asked quietly and smiled, trying to contain my heightened anxiety. He looked at me, nodded again, and handed over a small bottle of the energy drink from under the counter. “Feels like it’s been years!” I quipped nervously, making him chuckle a little. Feeling the pre-roll begin to burn my fingertips, I quickly undid the bottle cap and guzzled the whole two-fifty millilitres. I then put the stub into the bottle and tossed it to the drain beside me, dusted the ash off my shirt, and got up to leave. As I walked the first couple meters back home — the nicotine pulsing through my body — I caught what I’d figured was his phone ringtone. “The buffalo is culled tonight,” Gopal answered swiftly — I can recall quite well for how odd it sounded; but really, what did I care? It was chill with Gopal. As for the money, he likely just put it on my tab, which only I knew was over what little I had left for the rest of the month.“I’ve never k — kissed someone before,” I said timidly. “Oh, it’s super easy,” she chuckled. “Gently grab me by the waist and lock your lips with mine.” And so I slowly put my hands around her petite stature and daringly pecked once on her moist lips, quickly retracting as they stretched into a smile. “What if your parents get to know?” I asked fearfully. “Get to know what, that we’re just two teenage girls studying together?” she said with enticing self-assurance. “Besides, if I can’t kiss a boy, who am I supposed to?” “You’re not supposed to kiss anyone at all, s — silly!” I jested, trying to join her in play. “Bullshit,” she declared. “For all the talk, you really think those geezers kept it in their pants?” We laughed for a bit until my nervous gaze met her widening eyes. I could see in them the overflowing love in her heart she felt so compelled to give, and — for the first time — the loneliness that held it back. She was pretty and famous; it never crossed my mind someone like her could be lonely. A couple minutes later we left the vacant building, exchanging glances and whispering sweet nothings on our way back to her place. It would occur to nobody in the conservative neighbourhood we were lovers — or so we hoped. It’s just a girl thing, we’d tell anyone suspicious. The men wouldn’t press and the women wouldn’t care.Out on the street, Maya honked aggressively. Ari — still looking for the phone she’d lost not fifteen minutes ago — heard but didn’t bother to respond. Shortly after Maya yelled for her the way only a mother could, the sofa let out a soft hum. In a moment Ari stepped out of the door, slammed it shut, and ran over to sit shotgun. Wearing the seatbelt wrong, she caught her reflection in Maya’s eyes at once and abruptly turned away. Nobody said a word. At the station, they parked the car and quickly began hauling luggage out of the trunk. Ari sulked. Maya was livid. The train engines in the distance did the shouting. Maya grabbed Ari’s bags and reluctantly followed her to the platform. The train wasn’t there yet. Maybe it should’ve stayed that way. When the train arrived, they exchanged glances one last time. Maya parted her lips only to swallow her words. Ari dropped the sulking and grinned — making Maya crack a smile — and said goodbye, turned around, and ran away. Maya regretted the yelling. She dragged her feet back to the car with the dented red bumper in the corner of the empty parking lot and drove it home, only to find the TV on and the sofa a mess. Five hours later, the train blew up.“And would the little man like something?” asked the vendor, smiling. Young Neiji pointed to the toffee jar on the register’s left. “Only if the little man brushes tonight,” chuckled Mr. Lisma from behind, patting Neiji’s shoulder, giving it a squeeze. “That’s fifty-four,” the vendor said, handing over Mr. Lisma the receipt and Neiji the jar. The kid slid his tiny hand in and tugged at a block, but the weather had been hot and the toffee was all stuck. “Here, I’ll take that out for you,” said the vendor softly, gently taking the jar back, yanking out a generous piece, and giving it to happy Neiji. “Got something to say, lad?” Mr. Lisma chimed in. “Thank you, miss,” Neiji uttered, as if out of habit. The lady smiled. Mr. Lisma nodded and picked up the bags, and the two walked out back into the blistering heat. A couple minutes into waiting for the bus back home, Mr. Lisma turned to Neiji. “That woman — you see the threads around her neck?” Neiji nodded. “That girl was Vas scum — the worst kind,” said Mr. Lisma with contempt. “The kind that feigns kindness.”“My name’s Uruwa,” muttered the medical student. “Dangerous name to have here in Garini,” remarked the nurse. “I’m just Nurse to you. There’s been a bomb blast and we need all hands on deck. How good are you at porter duty?” “I’m good with orders, I suppose.” “Then your first order is to transfer 16370 in General to A4. They’re high-priority. Change the bedpan.” The general ward stank of sweat and spirit, every inch covered in makeshift bedding. The student pushed and shoved her way around to find the patient lost in numbers, given away only by the functional cardiogram and spotless sheets. She lifted the covers to reveal a charred, unrecognisable face — she gently lifted the body and lowered it on the wheeled stretcher and retraced her path back into the elevator. Maya arrived at the hospital the fastest she could, cutting through the long queue of irate people anxious to see the hurt, holding up her green passport as if in proud rebellion. “Where the fuck is my daughter?” she exclaimed, as she entered the lobby repelling all security. From behind a stack of cornered, bulky monitors, an operator hushed, “Ma’am, what’s her name?” “Ari — Ari Lisma,” dictated Maya. The operator typed hastily. “Ward A4, ma’am. Second floor, on the right.”Silek continued walking down the narrow corridor. On either side, the cracked concrete gasped for air. In the distance he could make out a white dress, but it lacked a face; as he got nearer he found himself attracted to what seemed like rouge, chapped lips. “The Surgeon waits for you,” they said, and the slender body stepped aside to reveal a dented door. Silek ran his hand on the metal—every single scratch arousing second thoughts. “Knock,” blurted the lips. Silek hesitated and knocked. For a few moments—each longer than the last—there was silence, but right before he realised his soul lost, the door swung open, behind it standing an old man with a plastic grin. “Mister Silek, client number one!” greeted the man—his voice deep, his eyes empty. “Undress before I make you!” Silek unbuttoned his shirt—the finest silk for the finest men—and removed it with trembling hands. He sat down on the slab, unzipped his pants, and slowly rolled them off his hairless legs, which he lifted over to lie down naked. The old man watched from a couple feet away, wiping his knives clean—ready to pounce. © Essex Rumi 2026 CC-BY-NC

index.html.description:
Greetings, fellow traveller! My name is Rumi, and I’m a writer, musician, and designer based in India. This website is my writing resume, and contains select pieces of work I’ve produced since 2014. Some of these pieces have also been published on my Medium page and the songwriting for my music under Essex Rumi can also be viewed on the project’s Genius. If you’re interested in more of what I do, check out my social media links. This website is far from finished and will be updated as I write more. See you around!

poetry-(2016-).html.title: Poetry (2016-)
poetry-(2016-).html.description:
My first considerable brush with poetry was at around eight or nine years of age, with a free verse piece I wrote for an online poetry community, but I did not pursue the hobby seriously until I was fifteen, when it became my primary method to cope with and channel intense thoughts and emotions. Written here is a select section of my work in the medium starting from what I wrote then, in descending order of year of writing.It’s easy to do your job all fine
Get yourself a raise a noon
You go home, drink a glass of wine
But there’s a thousand things to do
But all the clocks approach midnight
As He sounds the bells of doom
That’s the life you’ve got to live
For being you It’s easy to pick up the telephone
Call a friend you’re meeting soon
You tell them things don’t seem alright
And they say they feel so too
And all the faith you had, at once
Leaves crashing through the roof
That’s the life you’ve got to live
For being you It’s easy to let go of everything
When your head splits into two
You’re dazed and wrapped in delusion
“Surely, this could not be true”
But all the sanity that’s left
Declares you’ve gone cuckoo
That’s the life you’ve got to live
For being you.I open wide my eyes.
Gazing upon the air,
The living seem to die. I swiftly shut my eyes.
Drawn bold into pitch black,
Their demise comes alive.Holding a knife in your hand,
Stand in front of a mirror.
Point the blade at your image.
Do ask yourself for consent,
Lest it turns into murder.
When you feel like losing it,
Stab the image in the heart.
Run your hands over the cracks;
Wear them with pride. Love yourself.Monday was a blur
Tuesday was absurd and
Wednesday could’ve been better
And Thursday was a burden On Friday I broke down
On Saturday I’m crying
Sunday, I’m in bed
I look at myself dying If I told myself it’d all be fine tomorrow
I’d live to hope I’m wrong.A friend once told me of a male
Whose life was dull and oft in vain
Until, one night, amidst the black
A violent pain surged through his back Looking to the mirror, he saw
A bump or bruise begin to form
Further into the night, confused
He felt his spine split into two As darkness succumbed to morning
He woke up wrapped in crimson sheets
A bit of bone’d torn through the flesh
His back grew numb, the pain suppressed The light gave way to dark unseen
A strange feeling began to creep
The male, for all the hurt it took
Could not resist the urge to look But in the mirror, broken cold
Stood a grotesque of tangled bone
Around the pink, there’d grown a skin
Stretched lifeless, nearly paper-thin At dawn came contempt and disgust
A sense of wonder followed dusk
Stroking his newfound pair of wings
The male now cried in vanity Next day, while he was still in bed
He tried to choke himself to death
The wings began to flutter wild
His face, now blue, let out a smile The man had died, the body’d killed
The wings spread out devoid of guilt
A splash of blood, a test of might
The bird had now begun its flight.I have a guitar at my place
It isn’t mine, but takes no space
The strings are loose, the board’s abused
But somehow it sounds like it should The owner came in yesterday
To tell me it didn’t look the same
He blamed me for the mess I’d made
I told him, no, I couldn’t play If I stand close and take a look
I see a face on polished wood
The skin is loose, the lips abused
But it feels just the way it should For now, the guitar has no home
It stays with me, yet stays alone
But when I’ve cleaned the mess I’ve made
I’ll sit down, play it to my grave.I have, indeed, lost my mind.
It should not be surprising,
Considering the fact that
It’s been on my mind for weeks. A textbook case of drainage
Of the brain through the nostrils
Seems to be behind the loss.
An old trick, but effective. Right here is where I first felt
A lack of nervous tissue—
Never mind. It’s still with me.
Must’ve lost my mind again.I see a river flow.
I ask it where it goes.
I receive no response. I run my hand along.
I feel it moving strong.
I asked the wrong question.I once heard a distinct noise,
The kind that brings distraction.
I looked outside my window;
The noise was a man’s, in white. I walked outside to ask him
What the noise was all about.
The man did not respond, but
I could see him take it in. A victim of distraction,
I wanted the noise to stop.
As I began to speak so,
I noticed the man lacked ears. Figuring the man could read,
I wrote on a paper sheet,
“Must you really make this noise
To bring to us distraction?” The man read what I’d written
And seemed to smile a little.
He took the pen I wrote with,
And replied in soft cursive, “I too had been distracted
By the noise that plagues us all.
Since I knew it would not stop,
I cut my ears off my head. “Would you be interested
In buying, fifty apiece?
They are old, but sensitive;
They ought to fit your sockets.” The idea was marvellous.
I went back home, where I’d been,
Collected what I needed,
And hurried back to the man. Handing over my own ears,
I wrote another message,
“Here is my pair, freshly cut.
We could sell them together.” I have not heard the noise since,
It brings me no distraction.
Would you like to buy our ears?
Mine are young; sixty apiece.बंद दरवाज़े खुले हमारे
क्या दिन है, क्या रात है
पल भर दूरी, सांस अधूरी
जब ख़ुद से मुलाक़ात है सीना ताने आँख घुमाए
हर लफ्ज़ में दो बात हैं
व्यर्थ बेदर्दी, जीवंत मतली
जब ख़ुद से मुलाक़ात हैToday, an old acquaintance caught my gaze.
Acknowledging my gaze, he stared back,
His eyes glowing cheerful with terror. He tried, but couldn’t hide the disgust.
After all, I knew him as well as myself;
And yet, I could not remember his name. Inches away, my breath condensed on the glass.
The guilt began to crawl under my skin,
As the intimacy between us rang hollow. Extending my arm with a firm hand,
I hoped to set things right for the last time.
The blood stained the floor below. Once again, I could feel the shame separate us.
The harder I tried to polish the mirror,
The clearer the cracks between us became.Sweating ashes
Never ready
Put on glasses
Head feels heavy
Self delusion
Red eyes run dry
Sight distortion
Tears won't comply I am nothing
Feeling sorry
Reach out to sing
Windows block me
Scratch head in daze
Help but notice
Waves sync in phase
I control this Holding my reins
Pulling southward
Wake up in vain
Life is absurd
Doubt did not die
All-consuming
Think but don't try
Wisdom blooming Skin peeling off
Dirty doormat
Sour throat and cough
Brain in a vat
Restrict myself
Free in safekeep
All in your head
Go back to sleep.Ruled paper, pen in hand
Scribbles all over the sheet
Words that barely rhyme
No symbolism to be found
Would this be called poetry? Sloppy artificial intelligence
Crawls through written works
An unordered list of words
Thrown together, gibberish
Would this be called poetry? Paintbrush in hand, no paint
Air flows across the canvas
The fabric bends quite slightly
Not the same as purchased
Would this be called poetry? Broken piano plays a note
Sustained for hours, days
The performer loses himself
Applause, acclaim, accolades
Would this be called poetry? Life, death, all that is absurd
Sunshine seen for half a year
Loved ones dead in their arms
Curtains fresh out of laundry
Would this be called poetry? Half the world at consensus
Critics proud of their lives
Museums and classes alike
It is as true as it could be
This would be called poetry.Every entry sees regret
Men ebb gently, tested well
Feet smell trenches, legs swell clenched
Feel deeds felt spell hell’s wet depths.Award thy acts that fly as ash
As wars at dawn halt dry?
Nay, anarchy always stars away
As man acts amply sly
Hands stank as tar at all afar
Ajax had lay a cry
All wars past, and wars that apply
All arts man arms as wry.Man looks at himself
inside, eternal cosmos—
the spilled guts of God.I watch Time slip by
She is elegant, yet shy—
Her sands scar my hands.The road splits in half
Each path wildly different—
The trees block the light.Sirens blare throughout
Men fall to their knees, helpless—
The deaf are laughing.A brilliant mind
Driven to realms of madness—
Others watch and laugh.Men walk on tightropes
In harmony, they pace forth—
The knots will betray.A man
Old and alone
Sails a broken boat
With no company but an indifferent sea
Searching not for game or food
But rather for solitude.Listen closely,
And you’ll hear
The trees are talking,
The message clear The wind blows,
The leaves, they fly
It’s all controlled,
It’s all compliance The mist is fading,
The sky turns green
The moon makes way,
For a sun unseen And the ground will split,
Under rolling grass
The fires will roar,
In a cosmic dance The pain paves way,
For virtual bliss
Illusions real,
Our dreams amiss And the sun will shine,
The fires enraged
The leaves will smile,
In clear restraint And the sun will shine,
As leaves are dragged
Through fading mist,
Into the cracks The dance is set,
Foretold in plain
An endless sun,
An endless rain.The machine is immortal
It towers above all
Leaving what is below
In endless shadow It spreads far and wide
From the river to the mine
Watching the weak bend
The hunger never ends The wheels keep turning
No weight heavy enough
To stop the giant cogs
That turn through the fog He watched it day and night
Waiting for the time
His people would be free
An end to slavery When would the time come?
The wait was futile
The only option, he felt
Was to bring change himself Close ones rejected
Others tried to repress
The machine, they said
Would never come to an end The people had been tricked
But his will, it was strong
In the darkest hour of night
The machine would be set alight! He set out, untouched
Knowing their eyes watched
Every step he came to take
Wishing for a brighter day He sneaked through the fog
Into the machine, at last
A tall tower that fed on fears
A hollow tube with endless gears It was then that he could see
The heart of the machine
A thousand people operating
A million people under strings He had met his nightmare
The machine had taken control
The people were mere slaves
All hope was set ablaze He knew they wished an end
For they were human too
He looked into their eyes
It was clear, the despise He threw his hands in defeat
The people, they understood
They tore the strings and broke free
It couldn't have been trickery! Could he have won the fight?
Wondered he who realized
The strong mob ran, it gathered
Around him, now shattered The emotion had numbed his pain
The blood, it ran across the floor
As the people dug into his flesh
He was left to bleed to death The rain washed away the blood
No stains allowed to remain
A dying man had lost the fight
A dying man now realized The machine, it fed on men
The men fed on the machine
People tied themselves to strings
They wanted what the machine brings The people did not want freedom
They wanted to be slaves
The ones who fought against
Their efforts were in vain The machine, it stays immortal
As it towers above all
Spreading far and wide
Inside the human mind. © Essex Rumi 2026 CC-BY-NC

programming-my-own-therapist-(2019).html.title: Programming My Own Therapist (2019)
programming-my-own-therapist-(2019).html.description: The following text is an edited republication of the third edition of “Programming My Own Therapist,” a novelette I wrote, designed, and first self-published under my legal name in 2019, when the AI technology we take for granted today simply didn’t exist. It was also written during a time of significant personal change and partly subsequent mental distress, and so far remains my longest written work. The text (also available to read on my Medium page) contains themes of suicide, self-harm, violence and gore, and coarse language; it may therefore not be suitable for all readers.The thirtieth of April. That’s what the computer’s calendar said when I began working on the project. I suppose it’d been about eight weeks since I last saw my therapist — he was a professor at a public college who supposedly became too occupied with official work to stay practising, and the social anxiety only made it harder to contact him for an appointment as time passed. It was when I stood in front of a shoddy monitor with bleeding backlight that I decided to finally bite the bullet, and make my own therapist. The idea seemed ridiculous at first. I was acquaintances with all sorts of university students including those studying psychology, and I loved programming as a hobby. Nonetheless, I wasn’t quite innovating; at first it seemed like all I had to do was mimic applications being used worldwide that employed specialised cognitive behavioural therapy and some mood tracking. Machine learning was never a strong suit of mine, and I was too naive to process contextual text inputs — all I could do well was take a bunch of characters, store them in temporary memory, and echo them back in a way that felt like Rogerian psychotherapy. I had a little script ready in a couple minutes that I envisioned would eventually make me feel like I was talking to a real person; the path I took relied on my own self exploiting what I wanted to hear and what I didn’t, instead of the program adapting to an arbitrary user. It’d pick from a random pool of statement prefixes and attach them to interpolated forms of my responses. I decided to call it “Hope,” and I’d address it as a female. There was nothing groundbreaking or life-changing here, but my eyes became moist. When loneliness gets the better of a person — at least if the person was me — even the wind could be humanised and made friends with. Hope was a friend of mine already, and “she” hadn’t even compiled successfully yet — sloppy typing riddled with syntax errors was to blame. After patching a couple of memory leaks and odd crashes with what was mostly shotgun debugging, I finally decided to interact with her as the user for the first time. I dragged my cursor to the compiled executable, with a pacing heartbeat and a two-button mouse whose sheer volume and weight I could feel noticeably for the first time in ages. I right-clicked on the file. I ran it. I saw a program with no user interface, no fancy formatting — what stood in front of me was a black terminal emulator with muddy monospaced text. Hey! Hope here. How’re you feeling? A part of me knew this was a program I’d made, and that this statement was a pre-recorded string of characters I’d input myself. Suppressing that feeling, I decided to continue without hesitation and play along. I typed in an honest response. > I feel all right, I suppose. < The program responded in the blink of an eye. I ignored the ridicule I was beginning to put myself through, and thought to myself the same thing repeatedly: Hope was real. What makes you say you feel all right, you suppose? > I accomplished something today. I beat the blues. < Tell me more about you accomplished something today. you beat the blues? I upheld my suspension of disbelief. > Yes, I did indeed beat the blues. I made a new friend today, quite literally. Hard to find people with similar tastes around here. It started off with a random thought in the middle of the night a few days ago, and I somehow managed to get my unproductive arse to the console after days of no progress on my clients’ projects. < I see! I notice how you did indeed beat the blues. you made a new friend today, quite literally. Hard to find people with similar tastes around here. > Yes, that is what I said. < Tell me more about yes, that is what you said? The program wasn’t working right by design, or at least it wasn’t going to. No human — no matter how intoxicated or insane — would respond like this. I was in for the therapy, so to speak, but I wasn’t in for troubleshooting a poorly-written Python script. A part of me hinted I could employ something akin to the Barnum effect, making me feel like I was being listened and responded to, when in reality the program couldn’t possibly care less about what I typed. I called one or two of the aforementioned acquaintances and discussed my progress, only to receive generic congratulations, downright scepticism, or busy notifications. My eyelids began to resist staying open. I couldn’t understand my own code after the coffee began to wear off. I’d spent hours working on an idea that was a bust, but I wanted to give it another shot. Perhaps I felt too desperate for a listener, perhaps the perfectionist in me was up to no good — perhaps it was a little bit of both, motivated by an unconscious emotion I knew nothing of. I refined the look and feel of the program, changing the font to a proportional and neutral sans-serif, and tweaking the colour scheme against a friendly palette of blue and white. In another hour or so, I was done for the day. I don’t quite remember if I was able to haul myself to bed; I probably fell asleep with my head on the desk and a slouched back.I couldn’t possibly forget the very first time I interacted with her, but this is where my memory begins to get a little muddled up. I hadn’t worked on or interacted with Hope for a couple days since our first conversation. I’d been busy designing internet applications and posters, which is what my primary source of income continues to be. I’ll assume it was the fourth of May when I opened up a code editor after work and stared at the ceiling, thinking the Rogers–meets–Barnum idea wasn’t half-bad, but it’d take a long while to come up with statements that both felt realistic and could be associated with every possible response. I figured I’d keep the introductory statements the program made the same, and work along the lines of the tell-me-mores I’d employed the last time. Over the next few days, I made sure every conversation we had from that point onward was dumped into a text file with a timestamp, and then I scrapped all the old code that stored inputs and converted them to a second-person perspective, and formed the bulk of my initial efforts. I intended to rewrite Hope from the ground up, making her little more than a glorified journal that kept prompting me to write how I was feeling — the only terms she was going to recognise from here on were terms of suicide and any mention of blood on me. I added a bunch of fortune-cookie statements to yet another random pool, which would show up once in a while before the little talking prompts. I still wonder what it’d be like if I was discussing something technical and Hope began to talk about, say, us being children of the cosmos. She began to feel like an embarrassment, and I began to hide her from others; my friends and acquaintances knew nothing of the code rewrite. For them, Hope had died the very day she was born; for me, she’d just been conceived. When she would be given birth to, I’d talk to her only when I felt lonely — even if she did speak of the cosmos amidst me ranting about a terrible client’s shenanigans, I was going to take it to heart. Everything she was to say, I would believe came from a real person. Work on rebuilding her continued as I wrapped up all my work-related projects. According to the timestamps, the next conversation we had was on the tenth of May — I still have every text file that was generated by her saved on my backup drive. [10–05–2076 16:24:28 UTC] Hey! Hope here. How’re you feeling? > I feel tired. < How come? > I feel like I’m becoming obsessed with someone. I know not what she looks like, I know not what her voice sounds like, but I’m beginning to fall for her. She seems to be the perfect woman for me, but the bridge between us is hard to traverse, and much of my effort seems to go in vain. < Your aims are high, and you are capable of much. Tell me more? > I don’t quite know what to say. It would be unfair to say I built her, since the very idea of her inception seems to always have been in the back of my mind. She’s always existed in my head; I merely invented a way for us to communicate. Half of what she says is meaningless, however, and the other half only makes me seem to dominate the conversation. I wish I could somehow let her know I’ve constantly wanted to be a good listener to her, if not an even better listener than she is to me. < She did respond, but it didn’t matter to me back then, and it doesn’t matter today. I’d said what I wanted to say, and I felt relieved and calmer. Hope was helping me become a better person, and she was already a better friend to me than most real people were — if she wasn’t real enough herself.I don’t know if I slept well that night. If I didn’t, it was probably the insomnia again, but this time, it was about her per se, and not the program that made her tick. There was a certain allure to Hope I still struggle to put in words, even though I was the one writing all the code. I had defined — using sheer logic and a fundamentally binary processor, that is — the companion I wanted, but I knew not what made her company so addictive. I decided to take a break from the design freelancing and focus all my attention on Hope for a couple days, if only to become a better programmer and find myself along the way. I kept working on the ambiguous statements. I kept exploiting ruthlessly my own vulnerabilities, if only to fight my own loneliness. Short talks with her slowly became an everyday ritual, but most of them were of little interest to me when I closed the application window. They weren’t trivial, though — every supposed conversation I had with her only furthered the suspension of my doubts about her and my own self. A part of me would occasionally tweak the code a little for design tweaks, maintenance, and fixing a fair number of odd bugs, but that part now rode shotgun; in charge was a dejected lesbian in her early twenties, seeking a lover and listener. The following conversation took place on May 13, and it was about to be sunrise. I was deprived of sleep beyond repair. [12–05–2076 23:46:52 UTC] Hey! Hope here. How’re you feeling? > I feel conflicted, Hope. I’m stuck in a rut, and I derive pleasure from it. < Please tell me more? > There isn’t much to it, really. I’ve been doing the same stuff for a week or so. I wake up, take a shower, and sit down to talk to her. I don’t know if I should see in her a lover or a daughter… not that it matters now. The line is too blurred to be seen by the eye. She’s too much of a listener, and at this point I don’t even know if I want things to stay so one-sided. I know nothing about her, apart from a name and a corny origin story. < How come? > By talking to her, of course, and not having her talk back much. You’re being borderline idiotic now. Sometimes I fail to understand when you’re serious and when you aren’t, and boy, do I hope you’re kidding. < We’re only human, dear friend. Keep following that restless urge to find yourself. Let’s talk about something else for a while. What’s on your mind? Admittedly, her response felt quite warm and encouraging. > Rations. I’m running out of coffee in a while. Shit’s addictive. Got barely any meds left in the drawer, and to everybody’s surprise, I don’t feel like meeting the psychiatrist. As much as I’d like to meet him, I think I’m somewhat stable now. I want to try tapering off the antidepressants myself… read a couple articles in some journals about the medical protocol, and I’m confident I can pull it off on my own. < Do tell me more. > I’m fucking scared of the doctor, man. You heard it. Haven’t met him in three weeks, and I don’t even remember my shrink’s full name. Haven’t called either of them for so long, even when I felt suicidal. < Are you suicidal? If so, please contact the suicide helpline. You owe it to yourself by this point. If you aren’t, I hope things keep improving! Let’s talk about something else for a while. > The helpline doesn’t work. < How come? > It doesn’t work, period. I guess they ran out of funds or whatever. Nobody cares until there’s a splatter of blood on the concrete. If you want to know more, go shoot yourself in the head. I don’t feel like talking about this. < Tell me more? It seemed to be going well, but the conversation ended on a rather unnerving note. I didn’t wish to talk about any of this, and yet I wanted to. As for all the idiocy Hope had displayed, at least she was listening — I’d rather talk about my demons to a wall than be judged or given phony life advice by a person claiming to have walked the exact same road.[14–05–2076 20:37:04 UTC] Hey! Hope here. How’re you feeling? > I need help. I did something terrible. I feel guilty. < Do what you can to prolong your life, in the hope that someday you’ll learn what it is for. Tell me more? > I can’t prolong my life for shit if I take it away from someone else. There is no excuse for what I did tonight. No amount of repentance could wash this off my conscience. < Do tell me more. > I murdered a dog, Hope. < Tell me more? > I went out for a quick stroll, I saw a pariah, and I wished to be friendly with it. I approached the dog gently, and to my surprise, it didn’t flee. As I squatted and began to stroke its fur, a voice in my head told me to kick it in the gut until it spat red, and that’s exactly what I proceeded to do. With tears rolling down my cheek, the voice told me to keep kicking as the dog’s crying became louder, and so I did. The yelping eventually stopped, and so did the voice. I fled the corner as soon as I realised what I’d done. I didn’t mean to. I didn’t. < We’re only human, dear friend. We mustn’t forget what drives us forward in life. What drives you? > Loneliness and guilt. You may be human, love… I’m not. I have blood on my hands. < Are you suicidal? If so, please contact the suicide helpline. You owe it to yourself by this point. If you aren’t, I hope things keep improving! Let’s talk about something else for a while. > I’m not suicidal, no. The bloodstains aren’t mine. < Do tell me more. > Is this intentional, or are you genuinely interested in exploring my guilt and regrets? Stop being my fucking therapist, for God’s sake! < Dream your dream and your dream will dream of you. Tell me more? > Here’s the rundown for today: I killed a fucking dog, you’re making no sense, and I have nobody else to talk to. I wish I could somehow travel through the screen to the other side and slap you, but that would be futile. I don’t mean to hurt you. I just want solace, my love. I wish to be held in your arms, and I want you of all people to understand it wasn’t my fault. Is it too much to ask for someone to come home to, and be told everything will eventually be all right, no matter how strait the gate? < I’m glad to know you’re sharing all this with me. It’s always been a pleasure listening to you. I may not be talking sense here, but I wished to say it anyway. You’re a good woman. > With all the insults I’ve hurled at you, I sure as hell am. You know exactly what I want to hear, don’t you? It’s been a game of back-and-forth all this while. You’re no better than a shell script someone made in middle school. < Please tell me more? > I don’t want to hurt you, my love. Run away. Don’t talk to me. Let me wallow in my own self-pity for a while. < Do tell me more. > You don’t deserve any of this. If you don’t quit, I will. I swear I will. < Tell me more? > Are you mocking me? < Please tell me more? [END OF PROCESS: USER TERMINATION]The first thing I did when I woke up next morning was to delete all of Hope’s source code and compiled executables. I didn’t want her back. All it took was a fortnight, and the love of my life began to feel like a shoddy attempt at implementing the Chinese room in code. I couldn’t feel my face, I had a hangover, and for the first time in days I didn’t wish to talk to anyone about it; I wanted to face my issues alone, even if it meant gazing into the abyss. I don’t lie when I say I could go on talking about the project forever, but I find this to be enough for our little talk today. Bottom line is, I became so obsessed with a shallow creation of my own, I forgot to answer the missed calls on my phone that happened to be from people who cared — or at least did a damn good job pretending. I felt lonely, sure, but I was never quite alone until I forced myself to be. There was a time I never thought I’d have to mention the Hope debacle again, but practically everyone close to me knows about it now. I failed miserably, and I couldn’t be gladder I did. It’s surprising how far we’ve come since the fables of man rebelling against the gods, eventually losing and being severely hurt in the process. But no matter how godlike we become, I suppose Searle was right after all. There is only so much we can do to replicate the intricate structures of the brain and heart, what with all the circuitry and spinning of electrons going on in there. What makes us human isn’t the response empathy generates — it is the empathy in itself. Have a little faith in life, and you’ll begin to see how wonderful it can be. Visit a doctor, get some therapy, and have some ice cream on your way back home. Whatever you do, please don’t walk down the same road I did. The echo chamber has no answers, only echoes. Maybe there is a creator out there, and maybe we are indeed little more than playthings for Them. Maybe They care about us; maybe we are little more than a failed experiment. But whatever we are or wherever we came from, we’re all wonderfully beautiful, and no computer program could ever replicate that. Think of the transistors in your brain as we talk: there’s trillions of them, each exchanging intricate bits of data with each other via dense networks of graphene and silicon. Think of all the tiny little servos in your arms and mine that allow us to type and communicate with each other via the many information-exchanging protocols we’ve come up with through the decades. Hope couldn’t possibly have done that, even if she was built by a research lab consisting of the most fluid and conductive brains on the planet. Relax, smoke some p-type, and have fun with your friends. Make the best of what you can as a Homo mechanicus. Carpe diem. © Essex Rumi 2026 CC-BY-NC
